sense.text:
Many grew up on John 3:16 like a national anthem, and they read verse 16 alone. They accuse us of cherry picking, but they never quote verse 14: “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up”.

“Even so” means the exact same way and for the exact same reason. The people Moses lifted up the serpent for in the wilderness were Israel, and Christ had to be lifted up for the same people.

Remember too that when Christ walked the earth and taught, there was no Gospel of John and there were no letters of Paul. The gospels are accounts given after he died, rose and went up to glory with his Father. Christ was not quoting John; John was recording what happened.

“That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” The apologist jumps on “whosoever” and says it means everybody. But the whosoever here is the same people verse 14 is talking about: the people the serpent was lifted up for in the wilderness.

“For God so loved the world”. The same whosoever of verse 15 is the whosoever of verse 16. So the verse is taken apart piece by piece, and the key word is “loved.”

Loved is past tense. I loved that movie: I saw it before. I loved that car: I had it before. So God loved this world before. The question is what world God loved before, and the Old Testament answers it. Nowhere does it say God loved the Moabites or the Canaanites, or that he made a promise to their forefathers. The love and the promise were to Israel’s fathers.

Many who sit in this truth are still covertly thinking the world really means the other nations. The apologists run to the Greek, to Blue Letter Bible and Strong’s, and use the Strong’s to bring forth their strong delusions. So go through the Bible and see whether hatred has made us blind, or whether the Bible itself says who the world is.

precepts.why:
“The Lord did not set his love upon you, nor choose you, because ye were more in number than any people; for ye were the fewest of all people”. The you is Israel. “But because the Lord loved you, and because he would keep the oath which he had sworn unto your fathers, hath the Lord brought you out with a mighty hand”.

The Lord loved us not because we were the greatest in number, but because of the oath he made with our forefathers. As a nation our people are vile and evil, and the only reason God has not destroyed us off this planet is the love he had for our forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. For their sakes we exist. Abraham was a friend of God, and God is a faithful friend: however evil and stupid we have been, he keeps his love for the patriarchs.

So that is the love John 3:16 speaks of. Nowhere in the Old Testament does God love the Moabites or the Canaanites, or make a promise with their forefathers.

“Only the Lord had a delight in thy fathers to love them, and he chose their seed after them, even you above all people, as it is this day.”

The Lord delighted in our fathers to love them, and because of that love he chose their seed after them, us, above all people. God loved Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that love passed on to us. That is what the love of John 3:16 is.

“When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.”

This is twofold. It goes to Christ first and foremost, who fled into Egypt from Herod, prophetically. And it is the Lord loving us: “I loved him.” When did he love us? Because of the promise he made to our forefathers. That is the world that God so loved, and it will be read again and again.

“But now thus saith the Lord that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine.” The Lord always reminded us and our forefathers how he took us out of bondage. He told Abraham he would deliver his seed, and because of the love he had for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and how faithful and righteous they were, that love passed on to us. In Egypt under hard bondage, God remembered the covenant he made with our forefathers.

“When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee”. That is going into Egypt and the deliverance: the Most High used Moses to part the Red Sea, we walked through the middle, and the water did not drown us; he was with us, the chariot over our heads. The rivers are Jordan.

“When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.” Why mention fire? Because the deliverance out of Egypt back then was through the water, and the deliverance out of this Egypt will be through the fire. When the nukes and bombs drop, we will be in the midst of it and not be taken; everyone else will burn and disintegrate. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego walked in the fiery furnace with an angel and nothing touched them: an allegory of what happens to us in this time. Speaking of bombs and missiles: the news showed a Hellfire missile, one of the most destructive there is, hitting a glowing flying object head on, a direct hit, and it bounced off like a ball and kept on going. The elites who run this world know what those things are, and they know they cannot stop them. They are terrified, and they should be, because there will be a bunch of those coming soon. This is war; they are coming for us, Esau, and they are coming for you too, and not the way you think.

“I gave Egypt for thy ransom, Ethiopia and Seba for thee.” He killed the Egyptians to deliver us, and destroyed those too. “Since thou wast precious in my sight, thou hast been honourable, and I have loved thee: therefore will I give men for thee, and people for thy life.” The thou is Israel. God is saying, I will kill nations for you to save you. Nowhere does he say I will kill Edom for Canaan or Ishmael for Ham. He delivers Israel out of the water and out of the fire, not all nations. Where do you get all nations from?

“The burden of the word of the Lord to Israel by Malachi. I have loved you, saith the Lord.” He has always loved us. “Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us?” We were always in captivity, always rebellious, always in slavery, so we ask, when did you love us? God answers by returning to the brothers: “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? saith the Lord: yet I loved Jacob, And I hated Esau”.

“And laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the dragons of the wilderness.” He gave Esau a mountainous land, and over time had Ishmael remove him out of the land. “Whereas Edom saith, We are impoverished”: conquered, in the Caucasus mountains, subjugated by Israel. “But we will return and build the desolate places”: that is the Renaissance, when the Italians began to rebuild and reestablish themselves. “They shall build, but I will throw down”: they rise, but he brings them down.

“And they shall call them, The border of wickedness”: this nation is the beginning and the end of all evil. All nations are wicked; there are evil vile black and brown devils all over the place, Nino Brown and Frank Lucas on steroids, and we spend more time dealing with them than the heathens. That is who Christ dealt with. Christ did not spend his time arguing with white folk. Meanwhile some of you are still in slavery under him, his face on your money, paying his taxes and his rent, carrying his last name and his license in your wallet, but him kissing your foot gives you solace.

“The people against whom the Lord hath indignation for ever.” People say hated means he preferred Esau less. So you tell your twin son, I don’t hate you, I just prefer you less? Damn you Christians are stupid. Indignation is a righteous anger, strong displeasure, and the first synonym given is resentment, and resentment is hatred. Throughout the whole Bible Esau is condemned, slaughtered and destroyed, despised from the moment he was born. There is no place where Edom is granted mercy. So the love of John 3:16 is the love for Jacob, not Esau.

sense.text:
“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” What is the Lamb of God, and who was the lamb for? The law answers it: a lamb was for each house of Israel. And John the Baptist got this from Isaiah 53, where the lamb is cut off for the transgression of “my people.”

So the world whose sin the Lamb takes away is Israel. It does not say Israel there, it says the world; the apologist sees the Bible through Caucasian lenses. But it is very clear where John got it from.

precepts.why:
“And the Lord spake unto Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, This month shall be unto you the beginning of months”. “Speak ye unto all the congregation of Israel, saying, In the tenth day of this month they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to the house of their fathers, a lamb for an house”.

The word was spoken to the congregation of Israel. Every tribe had to have a lamb, according to the house of their fathers. Not a lamb for Egypt, a lamb for Ishmael, a lamb for the Ammonites, but a lamb for Judah, a lamb for Benjamin, a lamb for Levi, a lamb for Ephraim. That is who the Lamb of God is for.

This is where John got “the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world”. “Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?” The arm of the Lord is Christ. “For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant”: he is Christ and before him is the Father. “And as a root out of a dry ground”: the dry ground is us. “He hath no form nor comeliness”: he would not be a pretty boy, desired for his looks. “He is despised and rejected of men”, and “we esteemed him not”: we refused to believe he was the arm of the Lord, being evil and rebellious, not all of us, but the elders. That is why it asks who hath believed our report.

“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken”: we saw him beaten and whipped. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities”. Isaiah is speaking about Israel. “All we like sheep have gone astray”: all we Israelites, who rejected him. “And the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all”: Israelites all, not all nations all.

“He is brought as a lamb to the slaughter”, and he opened not his mouth: he was sentenced and said nothing, he did not argue or fight. “He was taken from prison and from judgment”, after the chief priests apprehended him. “For he was cut off out of the land of the living”: he was killed. Keep that in mind. And for whom? “For the transgression of my people was he stricken.” My people.

“And he made his grave with the wicked”: the two malefactors on both sides. “And with the rich in his death”: Joseph of Arimathaea. “Because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth”: he was innocent. “When thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin”. “By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities”: going back to the transgression of my people. Isaiah did not say the transgression of all nations.

“And he shall divide the spoil with the strong”: the 144,000. “And he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors”: he became our mediator, our intercessor, and the transgressors are the transgressors of verse 8, his people. So behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world: the world there is the Israelites.

“Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”. Seventy weeks is 490 years, upon Daniel’s people, Israel. “To finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity”: Christ died to make an end of sins and to make reconciliation for our iniquity. Keep that word reconciliation in mind. “And to anoint the most Holy”: the most Holy is Christ.

“From the going forth of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince”: from the time of Persia, of Ezra and Nehemiah, to Christ was 400 years. “And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”: cut off from the land of the living, just as Isaiah said. He was not killed for himself; he died for the sins of many, his people.

“And the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary”: the prince is Titus of Rome. This is not the time of the Greeks. The Greeks defiled the temple, and we went back in with the Hasmonean family and cleansed it; it was still standing. This prophecy is the temple destroyed after Christ died, not defiled. “And the end thereof shall be with a flood”: the flood is war, a seven year war. “And unto the end of the war desolations are determined”: us removed out of the land and heathens walking upon it up to this very day.

So here is a question for the apologists who believe the people over in Israel today are the rightful possessors of the land. The Bible says the righteous of Israel will be put back in the land, and that the nations will come to them to learn how to serve God. So are all nations going to come to them to learn how to bomb innocent men, women and children? If they are the people of prophecy, you support whatever they do there, and you are an ally to genocide. If what they are doing is wrong, then they do not fit prophecy and they cannot be the people: they are impostors, counterfeits, as we have taught for decades. Either way you lose. And the ones who refuse to answer that question, more than likely they are in bed with them.

sense.text:
The love part is plain; now the world part. The apologists will run to the Greek: the word world in John 3:16 is G2889, kosmos, and its list of meanings includes the inhabitants of the earth, the human family, even the Gentiles as contrasted with the Jews. So, they say, God loved everybody.

But where in the Old Testament, which Christ taught from, can that be found? Christ was not quoting John or Paul or Matthew. The same word kosmos is used for the world in John 1:29, John 3:16 and 17, and John 12:19, so follow it through John and see who the Bible itself calls the world. And Israel is not found anywhere on that list of definitions, or is it?

precepts.why:
“For had ye believed Moses, ye would have believed me: for he wrote of me. But if ye believe not his writings, how shall ye believe my words?”

When Christ taught, he taught from Moses and the prophets. The prophets did not sit around negating what Moses said; they built upon the foundation Moses laid. So the words of Moses were the words of Christ. Who do you think gave Moses those laws in the first place? Who was Moses talking to that whole time? Not Christ’s Father: our Father, Christ. We were talking to Dad, and Christ’s Father is Grandpa.

So when we read the words of Moses or the prophets, where do we find him saying he loves all the nations, or that he sent his son to die for all the nations? You will not find it.

“Much people of the Jews therefore knew that he was there: and they came not for Jesus’ sake only, but that they might see Lazarus also, whom he had raised from the dead.” This is six days before the Passover, in Bethany. Everyone knew Lazarus was dead, so they came to see with their own eyes whether he was really alive.

“But the chief priests consulted that they might put Lazarus also to death”: black devils, going to kill Lazarus a second time. “Because that by reason of him many of the Jews went away, and believed on Jesus.” Keep that in mind: many of the Jews believed on Christ because he raised Lazarus.

Then read on: “For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle. The Pharisees therefore said among themselves, Perceive ye how ye prevail nothing? behold, the world is gone after him.” We are losing our following. What world went after Christ because of Lazarus? Were all nations there? Verse 11 tells you: many of the Jews went away and believed. So the Pharisees called the Jews the world. The cosmos. We are the world, and not the Michael Jackson song; the biblical world.

“But Israel shall be saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation: ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end.” Israel is a world without end.

Some say that is a mistranslation and the word there is ages without end. No problem: the Pharisees still called Israel the world. And to the heathens in the comments saying nations are going to be saved too: of course you will be saved. Relax. You play a vital role in the kingdom of God, and what that role is comes at the end.

“Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing.”

He spoke openly to the world in the synagogue and in the temple, where the Jews always resort. What world was in the temple? Were the Chinese and the Arabs in there? No. So the Pharisees called Israel the world, and Christ called Israel the world. And the word there is the same G2889, kosmos. So Israel is a cosmos.

sense.text: “For this cause the people also met him, for that they heard that he had done this miracle.” The Pharisees were losing their following: “behold, the world is gone after him.” The world there is the Jews who went after Christ because of Lazarus.

“And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast”. Why are there Greeks among the Jews, worshipping at the feast? Who are these Greeks? The margin of the King James sends you to John 7:35, where the Greeks are the dispersed.

In the Greek the word is Hellen, number 1672. A Greek by nationality, but in a wider sense all nations, not Jews, who made the language, customs and learning of the Greeks their own, and the primary reference is to a difference of religion and worship. So a Greek was not only one born Greek: whoever took up the religion and worship of the Greeks became a Greek.

These Greeks were our own people, scattered abroad and Hellenized, who had come back to keep the customs of their forefathers, called proselytes. You cannot tell me the Greeks of John 12:20 are actual Gentiles.

precepts.why:
“Then said the Jews among themselves, Whither will he go, that we shall not find him?” They followed Christ everywhere, like people do us, harassing. “Will he go unto the dispersed among the Gentiles, and teach the Gentiles?”

Will he go and teach the scattered among the Gentiles? The Gentiles here are the dispersed: the word Gentiles here is Israelites. And the margin reads Greeks: it is the same word, Hellen, used for the Greeks in John 12:20. So Gentiles and Greeks are synonymous, used of the same people.

Other versions say it plainly: will he go to the dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? Will he go where our people live scattered among the Greeks? Because the Greeks are the dispersion. The dispersion are called Greeks and Gentiles: the children of God scattered abroad.

“If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him”, and all men there is not all nations. “And the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.” Then Caiaphas: “it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” One man dying for the people, by the prophecy of Daniel 9 and Isaiah 53.

“And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.”

That nation is Judah, the Jews. And the children of God scattered abroad are the Gentiles of John 7:35: the dispersed. So the Greeks who came to the feast are the children of God scattered abroad.

“They went both together into the synagogue of the Jews, and so spake, that a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles”.

The Jews and the Greeks here were both Israelites, Greek speaking Jews and Jews alike, in the same synagogue. These are the same Greeks who came up to worship in John 12:20: Israelites scattered abroad who made the language, religion and worship of the Greeks their own, and so fell under the name Greeks, Hellenes.

“A certain disciple was there, named Timotheus, the son of a certain woman, which was a Jewess, and believed; but his father was a Greek”.

Timothy’s father was a Greek: a pagan, but an Israelite too. The same kind of Greek as the ones in John 12:20.

“Moreover king Antiochus wrote to his whole kingdom, that all should be one people, And every one should leave his laws”. All become one people, all become Greeks, the way everyone in America becomes an American: Chinese American, Italian American, African American.

“Yea, many also of the Israelites consented to his religion, and sacrificed unto idols, and profaned the sabbath.” They changed their religion and worship and turned into Greeks: that is the primary meaning of Greeks. And the Greeks who came to worship at the feast had converted back to the customs of their forefathers.

Second Maccabees gives more detail about that consenting. “The king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to live after the laws of God”: to force them to change their religion and worship into the Greek fashions and become Hellenized, assimilated.

“And to pollute also the temple in Jerusalem, and to call it the temple of Jupiter Olympius”: polluted, not destroyed; it was destroyed in the time of the Romans. Jupiter is Zeus. Then verse 6: “Neither was it lawful for a man to keep sabbath days or ancient feasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Jew.”

We were forbidden to profess ourselves Jews. We became Greeks, willingly or by force. As the years went on and Rome came to power, Jews born and raised in those customs grew up as Greeks, with Greek names and Greek ways, but they were still our people. That is who Paul was speaking of, and who the Jews meant in John 7:35: the dispersion among the Gentiles, our people called Greeks or Gentiles.

sense.text:
“What then? are we better than they? No, in no wise: for we have before proved both Jews and Gentiles, that they are all under sin”. The they are the Jews, and Paul says no.

How have they before proved that Jews and Gentiles are all under sin? Where would you go to prove it? Where in the Old Testament are all nations and Israel under the same sin, all nations following behind Moses’ law? It is proven in the scriptures about all Israel, because the Jews and the Gentiles are both Israel.

precepts.why:
“Yea, all Israel have transgressed thy law, even by departing, that they might not obey thy voice; therefore the curse is poured upon us, and the oath that is written in the law of Moses the servant of God, because we have sinned against him.”

All Israel, not all nations; the curse is poured upon us. Moses gave the covenant and the commandments to all Israel, and all Israel transgressed. That is how the Jews and Gentiles are proven to be all under sin: the whole nation was under sin, as Caiaphas spoke of the whole nation in John 11. Paul proves it from the law of Moses.

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.” The same word for Greeks found in John 7:35 and John 12:20 is here. Paul is writing to you who are all one: Jews and Greeks.

Go up to verse 22: “But the scripture hath concluded all under sin”. That is Romans 3:9 again. What scripture? Daniel 9: all Israel have transgressed. “But before faith came, we were kept under the law”: who was kept under the law? The Israelites, who broke the law they were under. “Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.” After faith is come “we are no longer under a schoolmaster”, for “ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.”

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” The heirs according to the promise are the Israelites. The Jews and the Greeks are the same exact people whatever their status, bond or free: the same nation that Christ died for.

sense.text:
“That he gave his only begotten Son”. Is that statement in the Old Testament, that God gave his son? Of course it is, in Isaiah 9. And there the government and the order of the Son’s kingdom answer what the world is.

Go back to the kosmos definitions, and definition number one is an apt and harmonious arrangement or constitution, order, government. That is the world of John 3:16: the government and order of the Israelites, the kingdom Christ establishes on the throne of David. Number one, the first definition, is the right one: not five, not eight.

precepts.why:
“For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given”. Unto us, Isaiah’s people: a child is begotten, a son is given. That is “he gave his only begotten Son.” “And the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.” This son is called the mighty God: Christ is a mighty God. And The everlasting Father, capital F, because he is our Father, our creator, and his Father is his creator. Keep in mind the Prince of Peace: peace between whom? That comes in Ephesians 2.

“Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever.” He is of Judah, on David’s throne. His government and his order: he orders it and establishes the kingdom of Israel with judgment and justice, not American justice but godly, theocratic justice. “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this”: the zeal of the Lord is the word of God.

So the world God so loved is government and order: kosmos, definition one, the harmonious constitution, order and government of the kingdom of Israel.

“Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.” The Lord there, in all capitals, is the Father. The righteous Branch is Christ, the same as the root out of a dry ground in Isaiah 53. Judgment and justice: Isaiah 9:7 again.

“In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely”: all twelve tribes in the kingdom. “And this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.” The king’s name, not the heavenly Father’s, who is in verse 5. The Son is called by the Father’s title, in all capitals: senior and junior. You love the Hebrew until the Bible comes out, then the confusion starts.

sense.text: “When at the first he lightly afflicted the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, and afterward did more grievously afflict her by the way of the sea, beyond Jordan, in Galilee of the nations.” Assyria afflicted them. Zebulun and Naphtali are children of Israel, the northern kingdom, and they were called Galilee of the nations.

“The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light”. Pay close attention: the people that walked in darkness are the people of verse 1, Zebulun and Naphtali, the northern kingdom. “They that dwell in the land of the shadow of death”: captivity. “Upon them hath the light shined”, and that light is Christ.

Read verse 6 and verse 8 side by side: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given”, and “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel.” The word is Christ. Into Jacob: not Ham, not Edom, not Moab, not Ammon, not Ishmael, Jacob. And it lighted upon Israel: upon them hath the light shined, verse 2.

“And all the people shall know”. Oh, see, all nations right there? No: “even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria, that say in the pride and stoutness of heart”. The northern kingdom. They had their own place of worship, but God says no, Christ will come and teach you; your worship is garbage. Ephraim, Samaria, Zebulun and Naphtali have seen a great light and they shall know it. How will they know? John 4 shows it.

precepts.why:
“I the Lord have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles”. The light shining on Israel again.

The thought continues in verse 7: “To open the blind eyes, to bring out the prisoners from the prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house.” Them that sit in darkness are Isaiah 9:1-2, the northern kingdom, brought out of the prison house of captivity. So the Gentiles here are them that sit in darkness: the northern kingdom, not all nations, whatever your stupid commentaries say. Damn what Esau’s commentary says; we are the people of God, and it is our book, not theirs.

“It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles”. The preserved are the elect of the tribes. It is the exact same thing as Isaiah 42:6: a light to the Gentiles.

They will say the tribes of Jacob there are all twelve, so the Gentiles must be other nations. Hold that, because the house of Jacob is not always all twelve.

“Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph.” Why are they separate? Is Joseph not Jacob’s son? Because Jacob there is Judah, the southern kingdom, and Joseph is Ephraim, the northern kingdom. The sons of Jacob are not always all twelve; sometimes it is some of the twelve, or three of them. So when Isaiah 49:6 speaks of the tribes of Jacob and then of a light to the Gentiles, Jacob can be Judah, and the Gentiles the northern kingdom, them that sat in darkness.

“And the house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame”. The house of Jacob is Judah and the house of Joseph is Ephraim, so the tribes or house of Jacob is not always all twelve. “And the house of Esau for stubble, and they shall kindle in them, and devour them; and there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau”: Esau will be completely eradicated off the earth.

Isaiah said all the people shall know, even Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria. “The woman saith unto him, I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ: when he is come, he will tell us all things.” She said, I know. The people of Samaria shall know. He will tell us all things, because he is that light that lighted upon them.

Then verse 42: “Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves, and know that this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world.” Even Ephraim knew. The Saviour of the world: the world of Israel.

sense.text:
“It was necessary that the word of God should first have been spoken to you”. Why was it necessary that the word be spoken first to the Jews? Because the prophets said Judah first; unlike Christians, the apostles followed the Old Testament and understood it.

“But seeing ye put it from you, and judge yourselves unworthy of everlasting life, lo, we turn to the Gentiles.” When you say these Gentiles are heathens, you are saying Paul and them went to teach the white man, the African, the Arab and the Filipino. No: they went to the northern kingdom scattered abroad, the Gentiles dispersed among the nations, and to the dispersed of Judah.

precepts.why: “The Lord also shall save the tents of Judah first”. The tents of Judah are the Jews, saved first, “that the glory of the house of David and the glory of the inhabitants of Jerusalem do not magnify themselves against Judah.” That is why the word had to be spoken to the Jews first.

“And this is the blessing of Judah: and he said, Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him unto his people”. That begins with Christ first and foremost, but it is also the tribe. “Let his hands be sufficient for him; and be thou an help to him from his enemies.”

The Lord knew that in the last days the Most High would raise up the tribe of Judah first, to go out and reach and find Israel scattered abroad. That is why Judah was to be taught first, and why the word went to the Jews first.

“The Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people”. His people, not all people, not every people, “from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.” That is where we went.

“And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The nations here are still Israel: the outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah, gathered together in one as Caiaphas said. The outcasts of Israel and the dispersed of Judah became known as nations, Gentiles. That is who Paul turned to.

“Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life.” Cornelius heard the word of God because he was our people.

“Now they which were scattered abroad upon the persecution that arose about Stephen travelled as far as Phenice, and Cyprus, and Antioch, preaching the word to none but unto the Jews only.” After Stephen was stoned, before Cornelius, they taught the Jews only, because of the prophecy of Zechariah 12:7: Judah first, and Judah would go and find his people and teach them.

sense.text: “As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.” The sheep he already had were of his own fold, Judah, because he was Judah.

“And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.” Where did Christ get this from, other sheep besides the ones he already dealt with, all becoming one fold under one shepherd? From Ezekiel 37 and Hosea 1. The other sheep are the northern kingdom.

precepts.why:
“Take thee one stick, and write upon it, For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions: then take another stick, and write upon it, For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim”. “And join them one to another into one stick”: that is grafting, Romans 11, making them one fold. When the people ask what this sign of the twelve tribes means: “I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick”.

“And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all”: one shepherd. “And they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”: they become one.

“And David my servant shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd”. Is that not what Christ said in John 10:16, one fold and one shepherd? So the other sheep are the northern kingdom, and the sheep he had were Judah.

“Call her name Lo–ruhamah: for I will no more have mercy upon the house of Israel; but I will utterly take them away.” The house of Israel here is the northern kingdom. “But I will have mercy upon the house of Judah”: the southern kingdom, the Jews. Hosea’s first child was a son, Jezreel; the second, a daughter named Lo–ruhamah, no mercy, signified that the northern kingdom would go into captivity first, before Judah, and receive no mercy.

“Call his name Lo–ammi: for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God.” If you are not God’s people and he is not your God, what are you called? A Gentile, a heathen, a stranger, uncircumcision, Greek, African American, Haitian, Jamaican. That is what we became.

“Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea”, and “in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God. Then shall the children of Judah and the children of Israel be gathered together, and appoint themselves one head”. Gathered together in one stick, as Ezekiel said, under one head, one shepherd. And it is what Caiaphas said: not for that nation only, but to gather together in one the children of God scattered abroad, John 11:51-52.

sense.text: “Even us, whom he hath called, not of the Jews only, but also of the Gentiles?” Not of the Jews only: as Caiaphas said, not that nation only. The apologist says, see, Jews and other nations. But read on and see which scripture Paul quotes to explain this calling of the Jews and the Gentiles. The cogs are starting to break.

“As he saith also in Osee, I will call them my people, which were not my people; and her beloved, which was not beloved.” Osee is Hosea. “There shall they be called the children of the living God.”

In Hosea 1 it was the house of Judah and the house of Israel. So who are the Jews? Judah. And who are the Gentiles? The house of Israel, the northern kingdom. When Paul quotes Judah and Ephraim being called and coming back together, he is speaking of the Jews and the Gentiles. Stupid as hell. It is elementary.

And write this down: the beloved is Israel.

“Esaias also crieth concerning Israel”. Concerning Israel, not concerning heathens. The Jews and Gentiles of verse 24 are Israel. “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved”: the same remnant as Isaiah 11:11.

“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus”. Paul writes to the saints at Ephesus, in Turkey. Who are the saints? The Psalms say why Paul calls these people saints.

precepts.why: “Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.” The saints are those who made a covenant with him by sacrifice: Israelites.

“He also exalteth the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints; even of the children of Israel, a people near unto him.”

The saints are the children of Israel and none else. We are the children of God, the saints of God, and nobody else: not the ridiculous saints of the Catholic church, St. Pablo, St. Julio, St. Chucky, St. Freddy Krueger. So Paul is writing to Israelites at Ephesus.

sense.text: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” Whom did God before ordain to walk in his commandments? Israelites. That is who Paul is talking to.

“Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh”. If you were born a heathen, how do you change into something else? If you are born a Gentile you are always a Gentile; your blood and your DNA do not change when you follow Christ. So these were Gentiles only in time past.

“Who are called Uncircumcision by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands”. The uncircumcision is the northern kingdom, and the circumcision is the southern kingdom, born and raised in the law. The northern kingdom was called uncircumcision because we took on the nature of the Greeks, the heathens: strangers, Gentiles, uncircumcision, Greeks.

“That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world”. Without God in the world is what 2 Chronicles 15:3 says of Israel. When Jeroboam set up idols the northern kingdom went way off; when Judah fell in line with the Lord, Ephraim began to follow after them, and when Judah went off, Ephraim stayed off.

“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Who was far off? Daniel 9:7 and Acts 2:39 answer it: the northern kingdom. Christ dying on the cross granted repentance to the whole kingdom to reunite all twelve tribes as one again. That is grafting.

“For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us”. He is the Prince of Peace of Isaiah 9:6. Peace between whom? Judah and Ephraim, who had a beef, a hatred and division between them. The both made one are Judah and Ephraim: Ezekiel 37, Hosea 1, John 10:15-16. That is the division Christ came to do away with. That is why you have these stupid FBA saying, they are not our people: that is what the Bible is talking about. Dumb idiots. And some of you BHIs too, saying those in Africa are Hamites, those in Madagascar are Hamites, when you never set foot in Africa.

“Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances”. By dying he abolished the enmity, the envy and hatred of Isaiah 11:13 that went back and forth between Judah and Ephraim. Under the old covenant the northern kingdom was condemned and could not return: Judah kept the temple, the priesthood and the sacrificing, while Ephraim remained scattered abroad in idolatry. When Christ died and ended the sacrifice, all twelve were granted a chance to come together again by faith in him and get the kingdom.

“For to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace”. Twain is two: one new man, one new nation of Israel, making peace between Judah and Ephraim.

“And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby”. What does reconcile mean? To bring back together something that was together before. If you and your wife separate and reconcile, you come back together because you were together before. When was God ever in union with the other nations, that he should be reconciled with them? That one word destroys your doctrine. Reconcile both: Judah and Ephraim, one body, one nation, no more two kingdoms, their hatred slain.

“And came and preached peace to you which were afar off, and to them that were nigh.” Did Christ preach to those far off, Ephraim and Samaria in John 4? Yes he did. And to those that were nigh, the Jews first, as Zechariah 12:7 says? Yes he did. One body, those far off and those nigh.

precepts.why:
“Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.” Israel there is the northern kingdom: without the true God, without God in the world, which is what Paul is quoting from in Ephesians 2:12.

Read down to verse 9: “And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.” The strangers with Judah and Benjamin were out of Ephraim, Manasseh and Simeon: the northern kingdom was called strangers, Gentiles. When Judah, under Asa, fell in line with the Lord, Ephraim followed after them.

“O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel, that are near, and that are far off”.

All Israel, near and far off: Judah near and Ephraim far off. So we know who was far off in Ephesians 2:13: the northern kingdom.

“For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” Not all people: unto you and your children. And those afar off are the northern kingdom, the same far off as Ephesians 2:13.

“The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.”

Judah and Ephraim had a beef, a division and hatred among them. By dying on the cross Christ grants them both repentance and a chance to come together in peace. That is the division Christ came to do away with: he is our peace, who hath made both one, and the enmity he abolished is this envy.

“He prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.”

That nation is Judah, those who are nigh. Not for Judah only, but to gather together in one, to reconcile, the children of God scattered abroad: the dispersed, the northern kingdom, those who are far off. Judah and Ephraim in one body.

sense.text:
This is their favorite scripture. “And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous”. Christ is our advocate with his Father; we never go to the Father directly, there is always a mediator.

And the apologists who run to the Septuagint should not run there at all, because it helps us more. The disciples used the Apocrypha too; they quoted Sirach and others many times.

“And he is the propitiation for our sins”. Propitiation means to conciliate, to win or regain the favor of a god or person by doing something that pleases them. Why regain? Because we have to regain our favor with God again, as reconcile means to bring back together.

“And not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.” See, brother, the whole world, you are shooting yourself in the foot. But we have been reading all day who the world is. Not for ours only is not for that nation only, as Caiaphas said: and the whole world is the whole family of Israel, all twelve tribes.

precepts.why:
“Hear this word that the Lord hath spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt”. The whole family: the whole world, the whole nation that should not perish, all twelve tribes.

“You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities”. The only world that God knows is the whole family of Israel. He punishes us for our iniquities and saves us through his Son: behold the Lamb of God which taketh away the sin of the world.

“And these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle: and they shall make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, and his sons”. These are the garments of Aaron and his sons.

Jump up to verse 15: “And thou shalt make the breastplate of judgment with cunning work”. In it “settings of stones, even four rows of stones”, three to a row: sardius, topaz and carbuncle; emerald, sapphire and diamond; ligure, agate and amethyst; beryl, onyx and jasper. “And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel”. So Aaron carried all twelve tribes on his breastplate.

“For in the long garment was the whole world, and in the four rows of the stones was the glory of the fathers graven, and thy Majesty upon the diadem of his head.”

In Aaron’s long garment was the whole world. The four rows of stones carried the fathers of the twelve tribes of Israel, and God’s title was on the plate upon his head. So the whole world is all Israelites. Not for that nation only, but for the sins of the whole world: the twelve tribes Aaron bore before God.

sense.text: This one is for the heathen in the comments who said the nations are going to be saved too. “But they shall serve the Lord their God, and David their king, whom I will raise up unto them.”

“Therefore fear thou not, O my servant Jacob, saith the Lord; neither be dismayed, O Israel: for, lo, I will save thee from afar”. He will save all twelve tribes from afar: not just the three killing Palestinians, not those building tunnels in Brooklyn.

“And thy seed from the land of their captivity; and Jacob shall return, and shall be in rest, and be quiet, and none shall make him afraid.” Jacob returns and is at rest in the kingdom.

precepts.why:
After Jacob returns: “Therefore all they that devour thee shall be devoured; and all thine adversaries, every one of them, shall go into captivity”. All of them, not just the bad ones: every one of them. “And they that spoil thee shall be a spoil, and all that prey upon thee will I give for a prey.”

You can shoot your Hellfire missile at our chariot all you want; it will not do a damn thing.

“Yea, all the people of the land shall bury them”: bury the destroyed nations. “And they shall sever out men of continual employment, passing through the land to bury with the passengers those that remain upon the face of the earth, to cleanse it”.

See, you are going to be saved, for just that purpose: continual employment. No days off. You want the health, dental and vision, you have to work hard.

“And the sons of strangers shall build up thy walls, and their kings shall minister unto thee: for in my wrath I smote thee, but in my favour have I had mercy on thee.” There it is: continual employment. “That men may bring unto thee the forces of the Gentiles, and that their kings may be brought.”

“For the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish”. The nation that will not serve us shall be destroyed. No resumes in that day: just show up and get hired on the spot.

“In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen”. The tabernacle of David is all twelve tribes reunited again under Christ: one king, one shepherd, one head. It had fallen, divided and destroyed. “And close up the breaches thereof”: graft them together as one again. “And I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old”: all twelve tribes reigning with their king over them, as in the days of David, Solomon, Hezekiah and Josiah, with Christ on the throne forever, executing justice and judgment.

After that takes place: “That they may possess the remnant of Edom, and of all the heathen, which are called by my name”. Once the tribes are reunited, all nations go into captivity, every last one, with continual employment. That is how the nations are saved.
